content.content:
Stream Parallel Guidance
When to use parallel streams
[Draft, 1 September 2014. For now, minimally formatted pending
placement decision.]
The java.util.streams framework supports data-driven operations on
collections and other sources. Most stream methods apply the same
operation to each data element. When multiple cores are available,
"data-driven" can become "data-parallel", by using
the parallelStream() method of a collection. But when
should you do this?
Consider using S.parallelStream().operation(F) instead
of S.stream().operation(F) when operations are
independent, and either computationally expensive or applied to many
elements of efficiently splittable data structures, or both. In more
detail:
 F, the per-element function (usually a lambda) is
independent: the computation for each element does not rely on or
impact that of any other element. (See the
stream package summary for further guidance about using stateless
non-interfering functions.)
 S, the source collection is efficiently splittable.  There
are a few other readily parallelizable stream sources besides
Collections, for example, java.util.SplittableRandom (for which you
can use the stream.parallel() method to parallelize). But
most sources based on IO are designed primarily for sequential use.
The total time to execute the sequential version exceeds
a minimum threshold. These days, the threshold is roughly (within a
factor of ten of) 100 microseconds across most platforms. You don't
need to measure this precisely though. You can estimate this well
enough in practice by multiplying N (the number of elements)
by Q (cost per element of F), in turn
guestimating Q as the number of operations or lines of code,
and then checking that N * Q is at least 10000. (If you are
feeling cowardly, add another zero or two.) So when
F is a tiny function like x -> x + 1, then it
would require N >= 10000 elements for parallel execution to
be worthwhile. And conversely, when F is a massive computation
like finding the best next move in a chess game, the
Q factor is so high that N doesn't matter so long as the
collection is completely splittable.
The streams framework does not (and cannot) enforce any of these.
If the computation is not independent, then running it in parallel
will not make any sense and might even be harmfully wrong. The other
criteria stem from three engineering issues and tradeoffs:
Start-up
 As processors have added cores over the years, most have also
added power control mechanisms that can make these cores slow to start
up, sometimes with additional overhead imposed by JVMs, OSes, and
hypervisors.  The threshold roughly approximates the time it might
take for enough cores to start processing parallel subtasks to be
worthwhile. Once they get started, parallel computations can be more
energy efficient than sequential (depending on various processor and
system details; see for example
this article by Federova et al).
Granularity
 Subdividing already small computations is rarely worthwhile.  The
framework normally splits up problems so that parts may be processed
by all available cores on a system. If there is practically nothing
for each core to do after starting, then the (mostly sequential)
start. On the other hand, when the per-element computations are
time-consuming, benefits are immediate when using an efficiently and
completely splittable collection such as an ArrayList.
Another way of saying all this is that using parallel() when there
is not enough computation to justify it might cost you around 100
microseconds, and using it when justified should save you at least
this much time (possibly hours for very large problems). The exact
costs and benefits vary over time and platforms, and also vary across
contexts. For example, running a tiny computation in parallel inside a
an abstract computational method that can be implemented in its
subclasses, possibly relying on other protected methods
provided by this class.
ForkJoinTasks should perform relatively small amounts of
computation. Large tasks should be split into smaller subtasks,
usually via recursive decomposition. As a very rough rule of thumb,
a task should perform more than 100 and less than 10000 basic
computational steps, and should avoid indefinite looping. If tasks
are too big, then parallelism cannot improve throughput. If too
small, then memory and internal task maintenance overhead may
overwhelm processing.

I didn't find any results that measure pure Java matrix multiplication against OpenBLAS or MKL in FLOPs per cycle. The results below are from C, C++, MLIR, and compiler studies, so treat them as context rather than a Java benchmark.

- **Vendor libraries are near peak.** One MLIR GEMM case study puts MKL and OpenBLAS at about 92% of peak, with BLIS at about 85%. Its hand-written kernel reached 49 GFLOPS, roughly 27% short of MKL or OpenBLAS.
- **Register tiling is the biggest single gain.** That same study found that the register-tiling step (unroll-and-jam) gave about a 10x speedup, and it credits OpenBLAS and BLIS with reusing the output matrix in registers. This is the same reuse strategy the study identifies as the key factor in those libraries.
- **Blocking, packing, and register tiling can get close.** A compiler-only study reports code that is 34% slower than OpenBLAS on an Intel Coffee Lake machine. Another line from the same paper says the BLAS baseline reaches almost 50 flops/cycle, almost 80% of peak.
- **A hand-tuned C kernel reached about 82% of peak.** An older course lecture reports that naive code ran at 3.3% of peak and a vendor library at 70%.
- **Measured peak efficiency for MKL.** One benchmark found MKL at 89% of the theoretical flop-limited peak on a Kaby Lake i7.

The most direct Java-relevant figure is the MLIR result showing the gap to OpenBLAS and MKL closes mainly through register tiling. For a Java-specific comparison, you would need to search for JMH benchmarks, the Vector API (jdk.incubator.vector), or work from the JVM's own intrinsics.

The search didn't turn up a recent, direct benchmark of a Java Vector API SGEMM micro-kernel against OpenBLAS. The closest results are older or vendor-sourced.

- **Intel white paper (2017):** Intel claims BLAS algorithms can run up to 3x to 4x faster when implemented using Vector API, and a SGEMM speedup of about 4.25x. These are vendor figures from an older JDK, and I couldn't check their methodology.
- **OpenJDK panama-dev thread (2021):** This is the most direct comparison. A developer reported a Vector API BLAS peaking around 15 GFLOPS, while OpenBLAS, which uses handwritten assembly, reached about 25 GFLOPS on the same machine. The developer attributed the gap mainly to the register-blocked inner tile (3x3 for the Vector API version versus 3x4 for OpenBLAS) and to OpenBLAS's deeper loop unrolling. The post also noted that the Vector API version needed a 3x3 tile to avoid spilling.
- **Fma usage:** A 2026 Java Code Geeks article on JEP 537 notes that a FloatVector is an ordinary heap object with an identity, so the compiler has to prove those temporaries can be eliminated to keep data in registers. That is a plausible reason micro-kernels can lag hand-tuned code, though the article doesn't benchmark against OpenBLAS.

Overall, the evidence points to Vector API kernels reaching a substantial fraction of OpenBLAS throughput (about 60% in the 2021 report), with the gap driven by register blocking and unrolling. It is not a current measurement, and the 3–4x claim comes from Intel's marketing. To get a current figure, you would need to benchmark a recent JDK with the incubator module against a current OpenBLAS build on the same hardware.

The search turned up several useful sources, but none gives a single definitive answer to "fastest." The most relevant are Richard Startin's posts on Java matrix multiplication.

- **Startin's "multiplying matrices fast and slow"**: He benchmarks a naive and a blocked Java implementation against LMS-generated code. He reports that LMS does a lot better than 5x blocked (6x-8x) on my Skylake laptop at 2.6GHz. He computes flops per cycle as size ^ 3 * 2 / CPU frequency Hz. The post also notes that C2 improvements such as better use of AVX2 and support for vectorised FMA matter for JDK 10.
- **Startin's "mmm revisited"**: He describes a simple vectorised Java implementation which can maintain intensity as matrix size increases. His benchmark table lists a blocked 64×64 run at 4.5916 flops/cycle. The post also says that the saxpy routine wins, with blocked fading fast after a middling start.
- **Startin's vectorised algorithms post**: He argues that C2 provides quite a lot of autovectorisation, which works very well sometimes, but the support is limited and brittle. He also says that data parallel code can be better optimised by C compilers, such as GCC, than C2.
- **Algorithmica's matmul case study**: This is a C/GCC source, not Java. It notes that Why can't the compiler auto-vectorizee the inner loop by itself? It also reports that after a transposition step, Both manually and auto-vectorized implementations perform roughly the same.
- **Official context**: The JEP 529 (Vector API) page states that the Vector API aims to improve the situation by providing a way to write complex vector algorithms in Java code, using the existing HotSpot auto-vectorizer but with a user model which makes vectorization far more predictable and robust.
- **Academic comparison**: A 2025 paper by Pavlovic et al. reports that the API achieves up to a 79.62% reduction compared to auto-vectorized code in executed instructions on AVX-512 processors.

**Takeaway:** The sources suggest that C2 auto-vectorization is unreliable for matrix multiplication. Explicit approaches such as the Vector API, or blocked and transposed layouts, do better. The sources do not establish which Java approach is fastest overall. The flops/cycle figures come from different machines and JDK versions, so they are not directly comparable.

8:    In a recent post, I took a look at matrix multiplication in pure Java, to see if it can go faster than reported in SIMD Intrinsics on Managed Language Runtimes. I found faster implementations than the paper’s benchmarks implied was possible. Nevertheless, I found that there were some limitations in Hotspot’s autovectoriser that I didn’t expect to see, even in JDK10. Were these limitations somehow fundamental, or can other compilers do better with essentially the same input?
52:My code actually doesn’t vectorise, even in JDK10, which really surprised me because the inner loop vectorises if the offsets are always zero. In any case, there is a simple hack involving the use of buffers, which unfortunately thrashes the cache, but narrows the field significantly.
70:I left the problem looking like this, with the “JDKX vectorised” lines using the algorithm above with a buffer hack:
72:The Java code is very easy to translate into C/C++. Before looking at performance I want to get an idea of what GCC’s autovectoriser does. I want to see the code generated at GCC optimisation level 3, with unrolled loops, FMA, and AVX2, which can be seen as follows:
73:g++ -mavx2 -mfma -march=native -funroll-loops -O3 -S mmul.cpp
213:g++ -mavx2 -mfma -march=native -funroll-loops -O3 mmul.cpp -o mmul.exe && ./mmul.exe > results.csv

349:To understand the problem space a bit better, I find out how fast matrix multiplication can get without domain expertise by handcrafting an algorithm with intrinsics. My laptop’s Skylake chip (turbo boost and hyperthreading disabled) is capable of 32 SP flops per cycle per core - Java and the LMS  implementation previously fell a long way short of that. It was difficult getting beyond 4f/c with Java, and LMS peaked at almost 6f/c before quickly tailing off. GCC autovectorisation achieved and maintained 7f/c.

429:This final implementation is fast, and is probably as good as I am going to manage, without reading papers. Subject: Learnings with the Vector API
Hello,
As part of my exploration of the Vector API, I've run into the following issues. I'm then turning to you to figure out what eventual limitation I'm hitting in Hotspot and that can be trivially alleviated, and whether it is worth in your opinion to implement missing APIs and optimizations.
For context, I've been using two BLAS (Basic Linear Algebra Subprograms) implementations: one using the Vector API [1], and one using plain Java 8/11 APIs and code [2]. You'll note that the code is laid out very similarly, both to make it easier to transpose the algorithm from the Java 8/11 implementation to the Vector API one by hand, but also in the hope to present enough information to the JIT that it can easily autovectorize the Java 8/11 implementation.
You can also find the appropriate JMH benchmarks at [3].
# `a * b + c` isn't optimized to `fma(a, b, c)` on supported hardware
Even though major platforms support FMA instructions (x86 and ARM at least), there is currently no optimization in Hotspot to automatically transform `a * b + c` into `fma(a, b, c)`. Hotspot _is_ aware of FMA as there is the UseFMA global check, and `Math.fma` is intrinsified in the correct instruction. But there seems to be no "auto-fmaization".
This code pattern is particularely common in Linear Algebra workloads (as you can attest by the number of `Math.fma` calls in [2] even though there is still room for more). And using a single FMA instruction over the two MUL+ADD instructions brings a 15-20% speedup on the specific workloads I've been looking at.
The only significant behaviour change I can observe is the increase in precision since you don't compound floating precision losses on two instructions (MUL+ADD) because you only do one instruction (FMA).
# No `Math.dot` operation
The dot product is an extremely common operation in Linear Algebra. It is, for example, the most time consuming operations in matrix-matrix multiplications which are at the core of current ML and AI workloads.
In both the Vector API and the Java 8/11 implementations, I've laid out near optimal unrolling of the different loops for the matrix-matrix multiply case, but I've been hitting limitations in Hotspot register allocator leading to uncessecary spilling. Having a dedicated `Math.dot` method (or equivalent like a LinearAlgebra.dot) taking two "matrices of arbitrary sizes" would allow to intrinsify this very specific operation. (By matrices of arbitrary sizes, the intrinsic should be optimized for matrices of size 3xk for A, and kx4 for B, with C += A * B.)
The maximum speed I'm observing on my machine with the Vector API implementation is in the order of 15 Gflops/seconds, while the OpenBLAS implementation (which uses handwritten assembly) runs in the order of 25 Gflops/seconds. The main difference between the code generated by Hotspot in both cases is the size of the inner-loop submatrix (3x3 for the Vector API implementation, 3x4 for OpenBLAS), and the unrolling of the inner-loop (none for the Vector API implementation, and more than 4 for OpenBLAS). Both the augmentation of size in the inner-loop submatrix and the unrolling alleviates the current bottleneck at the microarchitecture level which is the high ratio of scalar instructions over vector instructions.
An intrinsic would allow to handroll a hardware-optimized dot-product, leading to performance equivalent to native libraries, and allowing any Java application doing ML and AI to accelerate some of their core operations in pure Java.
# Uncessary spilling in register allocator
As alluded to in the previous point, I'm unable to reach peak performance when doing matrices dot-product because Hotspot generates uncessary register spilling.

    Multiplying Matrices, Fast and Slow
      Dec 31, 2017
      | Richard Startin | javavectorRSS
    I recently read a very interesting blog post about exposing Intel SIMD intrinsics via a fork of the Scala compiler (scala-virtualized), which reports multiplicative improvements in throughput ov
8:    I recently read a very interesting blog post about exposing Intel SIMD intrinsics via a fork of the Scala compiler (scala-virtualized), which reports multiplicative improvements in throughput over HotSpot JIT compiled code. The academic paper (SIMD Intrinsics on Managed Language Runtimes), which has been accepted at CGO 2018, proposes a powerful alternative to the traditional JVM approach of pairing dumb programmers with a (hopefully) smart JIT compiler. Lightweight Modular Staging (LMS) allows the generation of an executable binary from a high level representation: handcrafted representations of vectorised algorithms, written in a dialect of Scala, can be compiled natively and later invoked with a single JNI call. This approach bypasses C2 without incurring excessive JNI costs. The freely available benchmarks can be easily run to reproduce the results in the paper, which is an achievement in itself, but some of the Java implementations used as baselines look less efficient than they could be. This post is about improving the efficiency of the Java matrix multiplication the LMS generated code is benchmarked against. Despite finding edge cases where autovectorisation fails, I find it is possible to get performance comparable to LMS with plain Java (and a JDK upgrade).
9:Two implementations of Java matrix multiplication are provided in the NGen benchmarks: JMMM.baseline - a naive but cache unfriendly matrix multiplication - and JMMM.blocked which is supplied as an improvement. JMMM.blocked is something of a local maximum because it does manual loop unrolling: this actually removes the trigger for autovectorisation analysis. I provide a simple and cache-efficient Java implementation (with the same asymptotic complexity, the improvement is just technical) and benchmark these implementations using JDK8 and the soon to be released JDK10 separately.
24:With JDK 1.8.0_131, the “fast” implementation is only 2x faster than the blocked algorithm; this is nowhere near fast enough to match LMS. In fact, LMS does a lot better than 5x blocked (6x-8x) on my Skylake laptop at 2.6GHz, and performs between 2x and 4x better than the improved implementation. Flops / Cycle is calculated as size ^ 3 * 2 / CPU frequency Hz.

97:JDK10 is about to be released so it’s worth looking at the effect of recent improvements to C2, including better use of AVX2 and support for vectorised FMA. Since LMS depends on scala-virtualized, which currently only supports Scala 2.11, the LMS implementation cannot be run with a more recent JDK so its performance running in JDK10 could only be extrapolated. Since its raison d’être is to bypass C2, it could be reasonably assumed it is insulated from JVM performance improvements (or regressions). Measurements of floating point operations per cycle provide a sensible comparison, in any case.
98:Moving away from ScalaMeter, I created a JMH benchmark to see how matrix multiplication behaves in JDK10.
169:          c[in + j] = Math.fma(aik,  b[kn + j], c[in + j]);

727:Interestingly, the blocked algorithm is now the worst native JVM implementation. The code generated by C2 got a lot faster, but peaks at 1.5 flops/cycle, which still doesn’t compete with LMS. Why? Taking a look at the assembly, it’s clear that the autovectoriser choked on the array offsets and produced scalar SSE2 code, just like the implementations in the paper. I wasn’t expecting this.

LMS is still faster when both matrices fit in L3 concurrently, but by percentage points rather than a multiple. The cost of the hacky array buffers gives the game up for small matrices.

1008:Given this improvement, it would be exciting to see how LMS can profit from JDK9 or JDK10 - does LMS provide the impetus to resume maintenance of scala-virtualized? L3 cache, which the LMS generated code seems to depend on for throughput, is typically shared between cores: a single thread rarely enjoys exclusive access. I would like to see benchmarks for the LMS generated code in the presence of concurrency.

The page doesn't contain the opening motivating examples you're asking for. The description's first section covers the patch size and a summary of the runtime-check approach. It never shows an `a[i+offset1] = b[i+offset2]` loop or spells out why C2 couldn't prove no-aliasing for same-type arrays.

The closest text is in the benchmark discussion and the performance-testing note:

- On the `differentIndex` benchmark cases, the author writes that they "only vectorizes with dynamic aliasing check."
- On the `sameIndex` cases, the author writes that "we already can prove that we can vectorize without checks. We already vectorized these before this patch."
- In the regular performance testing note, the author says a loop had "the load and the store have different invariants, which requires aliasing analysis runtime checks to prove that the load and store do not alias."

So, per the page, loops where the load and store use different invariants could not be vectorized without a runtime aliasing check. The page doesn't give more detail on the specific pre-patch failure modes. For the exact motivating examples, the PR's full description or the linked JBS issue JDK-8324751 would be the place to check.

Links: [{"title":"RFR: 8324751: C2 SuperWord: Aliasing Analysis runtime check [v18]","url":"https://mail.openjdk.org/pipermail/hotspot-compiler-dev/2025-August/095698.html"},{"title":"RFR: 8324751: C2 SuperWord: Aliasing Analysis runtime check [v11]","url":"https://mail.openjdk.org/pipermail/hotspot-compiler-dev/2025-August/095529.html"},{"title":"RFR: 8324751: C2 SuperWord: Aliasing Analysis runtime check","url":"https://mail.openjdk.org/pipermail/hotspot-compiler-dev/2025-June/093182.html"},{"title":"eme64.github.io","url":"https://eme64.github.io/blog/2026/01/14/Aliasing.html"},{"title":"RFR: 8324751: C2 SuperWord: Aliasing Analysis runtime check [v22]","url":"https://mail.openjdk.org/pipermail/hotspot-compiler-dev/2025-August/095764.html"},{"title":"JDK 8366274","url":"https://bugs.openjdk.org/browse/JDK-8366274"},{"title":"RFR: 8324751: C2 SuperWord: Aliasing Analysis runtime check [v23]","url":"https://mail.openjdk.org/pipermail/hotspot-compiler-dev/2025-August/095874.html"},{"title":"RFR: 8324751: C2 SuperWord: Aliasing Analysis runtime check [v23]","url":"https://mail.openjdk.org/pipermail/hotspot-compiler-dev/2025-August/095766.html"},{"title":"RFR: 8324751: C2 SuperWord: Aliasing Analysis runtime check [v18]","url":"https://mail.openjdk.org/pipermail/hotspot-compiler-dev/2025-August/095527.html"},{"title":"RFR: 8324751: C2 SuperWord: Aliasing Analysis runtime check [v17]","url":"https://mail.openjdk.org/pipermail/hotspot-compiler-dev/2025-August/095492.html"}]

The search turned up the JDK change behind this: JDK-8324751, the C2 SuperWord aliasing analysis runtime check, which shipped in JDK 26.

- **Why it was needed:** A quick investigation showed that it had at least one loop where the load and the store have different invariants, which requires aliasing analysis runtime checks to prove that the load and store do not alias.
- **How it works:** The author's blog says that while we cannot prove non-aliasing at compile-time for many cases, we can check for non-aliasing at runtime (for a small overhead). We check if there is aliasing/overlap, and only if the check passes do we enter the vectorized loop. Because C2 is a JIT, it can speculate that the aliasing runtime check never fails.
- **Two-stage fallback:** Per the review thread, the plan is to first use predicate and only generate vectorized loop, and if the predicate deopts, then use multiversioning. Without a predicate, we use multiversioning, i.e. we have a fast_loop where there is no aliasing, and hence vectorization. And a slow_loop if the check fails, with no vectorization.
- **Known regressions:** JDK-8366274 tracks cases where we have only aliasing, where we always end up multiversioning and taking the slow-path. The blog also reports slight regressions, which is a known issue with our auto vectorization approach, and under active investigation for very small sizes (around 10 bytes). The bug lists workarounds: -XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions -XX:-UseAutoVectorizationSpeculativeAliasingChecks to disable the check, or -XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions -XX:-LoopMultiversioning to disable only multiversioning.

The sources are mostly OpenJDK mailing list posts and bug tracker entries from mid-2025, plus the author's January 2026 blog. I didn't find a JDK 26 release note, so the claim that it shipped in JDK 26 rests on the blog and the bug's "26" fix-version field.

JDK26: Auto Vectorization and Aliasing | Emanuel’s Blog
  Emanuel's Blog
        Emanuel's Hotspot JVM C2 Blog
    JDK26: Auto Vectorization and Aliasing
      Jan 14, 2026
    Aliasing is one of the biggest obstacles to vectorization and auto vectorization in particular.
As we will see further below, it is also relevant for uses of the Vector API.
Definition Aliasing: two memory accesses are said to alias if their accessed memory regions overlap.
As we will see, auto vectorization requires the reordering of loads and stores. Reordering a load and
a store, or reordering two stores is only safe if these two memory accesses do not alias (overlap).
Let’s take it step by step and start with an example:
for (int i = init; i < limit; i++) {
    b[i] = a[i];
}
To auto vectorize the loop above, we first unroll the loop, and then reorder the loads and stores,
and pack them into vectorized loads and stores:
But how can we prove that the reordering is ok, i.e. that we can move all the loads to the top and the
stores to the bottom?
If a and b refer to different arrays, we know that the loads are not affected by the stores,
and thus it is ok to move the loads to the top.
If a = b, then we need to look at the indices of the array accesses.
We can see that the element i is only accessed in iteration i, and the element i+1 only in iteration i+1.
This means that operations of different iterations cannot interfere with each other, and thus we can
move all the loads to the top.
When the Compiler cannot prove that there is no Aliasing
Now let’s look at another example where reordering could be problematic:
for (int i = init; i < limit; i++) {
    b[i] = a[i + offset];
}
If the two references a and b point to different arrays, we can vectorize without any concerns.
But the compiler may not be able to prove that a and b do not alias, i.e. point to the same array.
For example, we may have the following scenario at runtime, where a = b and offset = -1,
in which case each iteration loads a value from the last element and copies it to the current one:
As visualized below, this means that the first element is copied forward in every iteration, so there is a dependency
between the iterations. The implication is that the iterations are decidedly not parallelizable, and so naive vectorization
will lead to wrong results, as we can see in the lower half of the graphic below. On the left, we depict the values
in the array before the execution of the loop, on the right the result. A correct execution copies the 0th element
with value 0 forward in each iteration, filling the whole array with 0. A wrongly vectorized execution copies
4 elements at a time, which leads to wrong results.
So even if it is very rare that a = b and the offset is such that vectorization leads to wrong results,
the compiler cannot just ignore that (faint) possibility - the generated code needs to be always correct!
For arrays, many loop shapes are “nice” where every iteration only accesses the i’th element,
and does not have such an arbitrary offset that makes compile-time aliasing analysis fail.
But for MemorySegments,
the problem is much worse: we cannot prove that there is no aliasing for even “nice” looking examples like these:
for (long i = 0; i < a.byteSize(); i++) {
    byte v = a.get(ValueLayout.JAVA_BYTE, i);
    b.set(ValueLayout.JAVA_BYTE, i, v);
}
Where with arrays, a and b are either different and have no overlap, or identical.
But for MemorySegments, the starting address is essentially arbitrary, and so a and b could also partially overlap:
This means that the problem of aliasing is even more pressing for MemorySegments than for arrays.
Aliasing Runtime Checks to the Rescue! (JDK26)
In JDK26, I was able to implement aliasing runtime checks (JDK-8324751).
While we cannot prove non-aliasing at compile-time for many cases, we can check for non-aliasing at runtime (for a small overhead).
We check if there is aliasing/overlap, and only if the check passes do we enter the vectorized loop.
But how to compute if there is aliasing? For each pair of memory accesses that we need to reorder and cannot prove
at compile-time that there is no aliasing, we have a formula that checks that there is no overlap.
So far, we have only vectorized memory accesses with a linear address form. Of course Java does not expose
addresses directly, but the compiler needs to convert accesses to arrays, MemorySegments etc. to addresses.
  byte array: a[i] -> a.base + con_offset_to_first_element + i
  int array: a[i + 10] -> a.base + con_offset_to_first_element + 4L * (i + 10)
  MemorySegment with off-heap memory: ms.get(ValueLayout.JAVA_DOUBLE_UNALIGNED, 8L * i) -> ms.address + 8L * i
In the examples above, we assume that i is the loop counter, and we can see that the address progresses
linearly as we increment i over the loop iterations. Let us visualize some examples, where each iteration has
two memory accesses that could possibly overlap:
We essentially have pairs of lines, or rather bands, as each memory access has a pointer where it starts
as well as a size. A little simplified, we get the following formulation:
  start1(i) = a1 * i + b1, and some size1, where the access in the i’th iteration goes to [start1, start1 + size1).
  start2(i) = a2 * i + b2, and some size2, where the access in the i’th iteration goes to [start2, start2 + size2).
  For all i in the loop range:
      start1(i) >= start2(i) + size2 or
      start1(i) + size1 <= start2(i)
This condition checks that either the first access always happens above the second, or the first access always happens below the second,
which implies that there cannot be any overlap.
Note that this condition goes over all iterations i, so we will generate a check that can be executed once before the loop.
If the check passes, we know that there is no aliasing for any loop iteration.
Note that we may need multiple such checks if there are multiple pairs of possibly aliasing memory references.

content.content:
Some examples:
  Fill pattern: only has one store per iteration, trivially no aliasing.
  Copy pattern: a load and a store, requires one check.
  Addition of two vectors: 2 loads and 1 store, two checks, one per load-store pair (load-load pair is always safe to reorder).
  4 stores: need check for each store-store pair, a total of 6 checks.
It is reasonable to assume that the aliasing check will fail only rarely. But what should we do if it does fail?
Many compilers resort to compiling two loops: one that is vectorized and one that stays scalar (non-vectorized).
I call this the multiversioning approach, where we have multiple versions of the loop,
that allows us to make assumptions for one loop (no aliasing) and optimize more aggressively (vectorize),
while the other loop has no assumptions and therefore fewer optimizations.
The downside with multiversioning is that we have more code, which means we spend more time compiling
and more code space, which can hurt instruction cache locality.
But since C2 is a JIT compiler, we have a powerful tool available: deoptimization!
We can speculate that the aliasing runtime check never fails. If the check passes,
we go to the vectorized loop. But if the check fails, we deoptimize, and go back
to the interpreter.
The benefit is that we spend less time compiling, and use up less code space and get better
instruction cache locality.
The downside of only using speculation and never multiversioning
is that if our speculation is ever wrong, if we
ever do encounter an aliasing case, we pay a high penalty:
we get the very slow performance of the interpreter,
which is much slower than the scalar (non-vectorized) loop we would have entered with multiversioning.
Both solutions on their own are not super satisfactory.
That is why we implement a hybrid approach that combines them both.
At first, we use the speculation/deoptimization approach, in the hope that the aliasing
assumption never fails. For most loops, this should always hold.
We get great performance, faster compilation and good code cache locality.
In the few cases where the assumption fails, we have to pay a penalty, but
would like to eventually reach great peak performance for both the aliasing
and non-aliasing case. So we deoptimize, and eventually recompile with
multiversioning. This way, we get the great vectorized performance for non-aliasing
cases, and still very good performance of the compiled scalar (non-vectorized) loop.
As we can see in the benchmarks of JDK-8324751, this leads to great speedups
for a lot of loop shapes, especially copy patterns for arrays and even more loop shapes
that use multiple MemorySegment accesses.
However, there are some 10-20% regressions for cases where we alias all the time (JDK-8366274).
I suspect that at least part of the explanation is due to lower instruction cache locality,
but I have not yet been able to do a thorough performance investigation.
In my opinion it is an acceptable regression for such an edge case:
as soon as we have any non-aliasing invocations of the loops mixed in, the speedups from vectorization
for those cases completely outweigh the small performance regression.
I ran the VectorBulkOperationsMemorySegment.copy_byte_loop benchmark
on my AVX512 laptop. We can see that with the new aliasing runtime check, JDK26 has significant speedups, especially
with byte array sizes above about 64 bytes. In the range around 10 bytes, here are some slight regressions,
which is a known issue with our auto vectorization approach, and under active investigation.
Aliasing and Vector API
If you are using the Vector API to speed up your code, you may have to consider the edge case of aliasing
and implement solutions for it yourself.

The search didn't turn up an integration announcement for JDK-8307084, so I can't confirm it has landed in mainline JDK. The results are all from the OpenJDK hotspot-compiler-dev mailing list, where the change is titled "C2: Vectorized drain loop is not executed for some small trip counts," with Fei Gao as author and Emanuel Peter reviewing.

- **The problem:** When the remaining trip count after the pre-loop is small but above the vector length, the vectorized drain loop can be skipped entirely by the main loop's minimum-trip guard. A loop with 25 iterations after the pre-loop may run 3 rounds of the vectorized drain loop, but that is impossible under the current code.
- **The proposed fix:** A new clone mode, `InsertVectorizedDrain`, is used when cloning the vector main loop into the drain loop, so the main loop's guard no longer jumps over the drain loop. The work is done in `insert_post_loop()`.
- **Latest activity I found:** A v4 revision from January 2026 is in the archive, along with a comment that a regression was filed (JDK-8368245) for benchmarks with small iteration counts. For very small iteration counts, it is faster to disable the auto vectorizer. A January 2026 thread also asks the author to sync with master and fix merge conflicts.

I found no record of a push to master, so treat its status as unknown. Checking the OpenJDK bug tracker entry for JDK-8307084 or the jdk master commit log would settle it.

The search turned up mailing-list threads from the OpenJDK Panama group, not formal benchmarks, and none covers JDK 24 directly.

- **June 2025, bound hoisting on JDK 25-era builds:** Chris Hegarty reported that a `MemorySegment` loop bound was not hoisted out of the loop, while array length was. His JMH numbers showed a plain array dot product at about 61 ns/op, versus about 99 ns/op for a heap segment and 95 ns/op for a native segment. The array load uses the int version of Objects.checkIndex, whereas the segment load uses the long version, which was one suspect. Maurizio Cimadamore saw similar numbers on x64. Disabling the Vector API's out-of-bounds check helped only a little (about 90 to 70 ns/op), and he said a single check hoisted out of the loop shouldn't cost 20ns, so he suspected a JIT problem.

- **Earlier, March 2024:** Maurizio suspected that segment bounds checks were not being hoisted, and noted that all the bound check analysis on memory segments is built on longs (unlike arrays and byte buffers). In his reply to a follow-up, he said that bound checks are correctly hoisted outside the loop, so the suggestion I made earlier is not going to make any difference. He had earlier noted that extra casts to `long` helped a related benchmark, because C2 could not yet optimize that loop shape.

- **September 2025, JDK 25 vs. JDK 26:** Antoine Chambille reported that auto-vectorization of loops over segments worked on JDK 26 builds but not on JDK 25. On JDK 25, a segment-to-array add ran at about 142 ns/op, versus about 218 ns/op for segment-to-segment. Maurizio attributed the fixes mainly to JDK-8324751, and said the main problem was that the vectorizer could not prove two segments were disjoint.

The thread does not give JDK 24 numbers or a clear fix version. The evidence points to segment loops being slower than arrays in JDK 25 and earlier, with improvements in JDK 26. For a definitive answer, check JDK-8324751 on the OpenJDK bug tracker and rerun your own JMH benchmark on JDK 24 and 25.

Hi,
I've been rewriting parts of our codebase which currently uses the 
Panama Vector API to provide optimised distance comparison functions for 
vector search algorithms. We previously used float[]'s which necessity a 
copy from our off-heap storage into the heap, so we simply want to use a 
MemorySegments to avoid this - since our stored vectors are in a file 
on-disk and mmapp'ed.
I see that using MemorySegment::byteSize as a loop bound is not as 
optimised as it could be. The bound is not getting hoisted out of the 
loop body, where it does when using array length.
I created a minimal jmh benchmark that demonstrates what I see

The removal is phased. JDK 23 introduced the deprecation, with warnings at compile time and at runtime. As of JDK 24, through JEP 498, runtime warnings become default. As of JDK 26 unsupported operations throw exceptions by default, and after JDK 26 the methods are removed entirely and the JVM ignores --sun-misc-unsafe-memory-access option.

For off-heap work, the suggested replacement is the FFM API. One source describes migrating such code to MemorySegment, with lifetimes managed through an Arena. A JEP 471 example shows an off-heap array copy replaced by using the standard Arena and MemorySegment APIs. A caution from the OpenJDK mailing list says the performance cost of Arena.ofShared() is 300x compared to Unsafe.allocate(), so that migration may not be a drop-in change for performance-sensitive code.

The results also include a JavaFX Marlin rasterizer change that replaces Unsafe memory access with FFM. That is a useful real-world reference, but it is not Agrona.

To find Agrona's actual status, check its GitHub repository directly for release notes and issues mentioning Unsafe, or search again using only "Agrona release notes" with the version you care about.

The search turned up a consistent phased plan, with one open question about JDK 27.

- **Phase 1 (JDK 23):** JEP 471 deprecated the memory-access methods, with the default set to `allow` (JDK 23 introduced deprecation with warnings at compile and runtime).
- **Phase 2 (JDK 24):** JEP 498 made runtime warnings the default, using `--sun-misc-unsafe-memory-access=warn` (As of JDK 24, through JEP 498, runtime warnings become default).
- **Phase 3 (JDK 26):** The default becomes `deny`, so unsupported calls throw exceptions. Inside.java says as of JDK 26 unsupported operations throw exceptions by default. The original JEP 471 plan also named phase 3 as throwing exceptions by default, in JDK 26 or later. The JEP 471 bug tracker entry says deny will be the default value in phase 3. It will be possible in phase 3 to revert the value from deny to an earlier mode. The option also has a `debug` value that throws `UnsupportedOperationException`, per JEP 498 (disallows use of the memory-access methods by throwing an UnsupportedOperationException on every occasion).
- **Phases 4–5 (JDK 27 and later):** The sources disagree on timing. The JEP 471 plan says removal happens in releases following JDK 26. Inside.java says after JDK 26 the methods are removed entirely and the JVM ignores --sun-misc-unsafe-memory-access option. JEP 498 says the option is ignored in phase 5, when all of the memory-access methods have been removed.

I didn't find a source confirming the final JDK 26 release status or the exact JDK 27 removal, so check the JDK 26 release notes and the JEP pages for the current status.

24:We will deprecate and remove the methods in phases, where each phase takes place in a separate JDK feature release:
34:Phase 1, via this JEP, in JDK 23;
35:Phase 2, issuing run-time warnings, in or before JDK 25;
36:Phase 3, throwing exceptions by default, in JDK 26 or later; and
37:Phases 4 and 5, which will remove the methods, in releases following JDK 26.
38:We may implement phases 4 and 5 simultaneously, if appropriate, when the time arrives.
50:The default value of the --sun-misc-unsafe-memory-access option will change from release to release as we proceed through the phases described above:
51:allow is the default value in phase 1, as if every invocation of the java launcher includes --sun-misc-unsafe-memory-access=allow.
52:warn will be the default value in phase 2. It will be possible in phase 2 to revert the value from warn to allow, thus avoiding the warning.
53:deny will be the default value in phase 3. It will be possible in phase 3 to revert the value from deny to warn in order to receive a warning rather than exceptions. It will not be possible to use allow to avoid the warning.
54:In phase 5, when all of the memory-access methods have been removed, --sun-misc-unsafe-memory-access will be ignored. Eventually it will be removed.

3715 agrona.md
Agrona
======

[![Javadocs](https://www.javadoc.io/badge/org.agrona/agrona.svg)](https://www.javadoc.io/static/org.agrona/agrona)
[![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/github/license/aeron-io/Agrona.svg)](https://github.com/aeron-io/agrona/blob/master/LICENSE)

[![Actions Status](https://github.com/aeron-io/agrona/workflows/Continuous%20Integration/badge.svg)](https://github.com/aeron-io/agrona/actions)
[![CodeQL Status](https://github.com/aeron-io/agrona/workflows/CodeQL/badge.svg)](https://github.com/aeron-io/agrona/actions)

Agrona provides a library of data structures and utility methods that are a common need when building high-performance 
applications in Java. Many of these utilities are used in the [Aeron](https://github.com/aeron-io/aeron) 
efficient reliable UDP unicast, multicast, and IPC message transport and provides high-performance buffer implementations
to support the [Simple Binary Encoding](https://github.com/aeron-io/simple-binary-encoding) Message Codec.

For the latest version information and changes see the [Change Log](https://github.com/aeron-io/agrona/wiki/Change-Log). 

The latest release and **downloads** can be found in [Maven Central](http://search.maven.org/#search%7Cga%7C1%7Cagrona).

Utilities Include:

* Buffers - Thread safe direct and atomic buffers for working with on and off heap memory with memory ordering semantics.
* Lists - Array backed lists of int/long primitives to avoid boxing.
* Maps - Open addressing and linear probing with int/long primitive keys to object reference values.
* Maps - Open addressing and linear probing with int/long primitive keys to int/long values.
* Sets - Open addressing and linear probing for int/long primitives and object references.
* Cache - Set Associative with int/long primitive keys to object reference values.
* Clocks - Clock implementations to abstract system clocks, allow caching, and enable testing.
* Queues - Lock-less implementations for low-latency applications.
* Ring/Broadcast Buffers - implemented off-heap for IPC communication.
* Simple Agent framework for concurrent services.
* Scalable Timer Wheel - For scheduling timers at a given deadline with O(1) register and cancel time.
* Code generation from annotated implementations specialised for primitive types.
* Off-heap counters implementation for application telemetry, position tracking, and coordination.
* Implementations of InputStream and OutputStream that can wrap direct buffers.
* DistinctErrorLog - A log of distinct errors to avoid filling disks with existing logging approaches.
* IdGenerator - Concurrent and distributed unique id generator employing a lock-less implementation of the Twitter Snowflake algorithm.

Build
-----

### Java Build

Build the project with [Gradle](http://gradle.org/) using this [build.gradle](https://github.com/aeron-io/agrona/blob/master/build.gradle) file.

You require the following to build Agrona:

* The Latest release of Java 17. Agrona is tested with Java 17, 21, 25 and the next available EA build.

Full clean and build:

    $ ./gradlew

content.content:
Stream.collect(Supplier, BiConsumer, BiConsumer)
sum
double sum()
Returns the sum of elements in this stream.
Summation is a special case of a reduction. If
floating-point summation were exact, this method would be
equivalent to:
    return reduce(0, Double::sum);
However, since floating-point summation is not exact, the above
code is not necessarily equivalent to the summation computation
done by this method.
The value of a floating-point sum is a function both
of the input values as well as the order of addition
operations. The order of addition operations of this method is
intentionally not defined to allow for implementation
flexibility to improve the speed and accuracy of the computed
result.
In particular, this method may be implemented using compensated
summation or other technique to reduce the error bound in the
numerical sum compared to a simple summation of double
values.
Because of the unspecified order of operations and the
possibility of using differing summation schemes, the output of
this method may vary on the same input elements.
Various conditions can result in a non-finite sum being
computed. This can occur even if the all the elements
being summed are finite. If any element is non-finite,
the sum will be non-finite:
If any element is a NaN, then the final sum will be
NaN.
If the elements contain one or more infinities, the
sum will be infinite or NaN.
If the elements contain infinities of opposite sign,
the sum will be NaN.
If the elements contain infinities of one sign and
an intermediate sum overflows to an infinity of the opposite
sign, the sum may be NaN.
It is possible for intermediate sums of finite values to
overflow into opposite-signed infinities; if that occurs, the
final sum will be NaN even if the elements are all
finite.

Links: [{"title":"mixed precision training  c9ccbd15","url":"https://object.cloud.sdsc.edu/v1/AUTH_da4962d3368042ac8337e2dfdd3e7bf3/ml-papers-txt/ICLR/2018/mixed_precision_training__c9ccbd15.txt"},{"title":"arxiv.org","url":"https://arxiv.org/pdf/1710.03740v1.pdf"},{"title":"Mixed Precision Training","url":"https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1710.03740"},{"title":"Mixed Precision Training","url":"https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2017arXiv171003740M"},{"title":"www.arxiv.org","url":"https://www.arxiv.org/pdf/1802.00930"},{"title":"Submitted 15 Feb 2018","url":"https://alphaxiv.org/abs/1710.03740v3"},{"title":"arxiv.org","url":"https://arxiv.org/abs/1710.03740"},{"title":"alphaxiv.org","url":"https://alphaxiv.org/overview/1710.03740v3"},{"title":"Large-Scale Deep Learning Optimizations: A Comprehensive Survey","url":"https://arxiv.org/pdf/2111.00856"},{"title":"Mixed Precision Training","url":"https://arxiv.org/pdf/1710.03740"}]

The search confirms the paper is *Mixed Precision Training* (Narang, Diamos, Elsen, Micikevicius, et al.), published at ICLR 2018 and available on arXiv as 1710.03740. It proposes three techniques that let networks train in FP16 while matching FP32 accuracy.

- **FP32 master weights:** The weights are kept in FP32 and updated there. Matching FP32 results required updating an FP32 master copy after the FP16 forward and backward passes, whereas updating FP16 weights caused about 80% relative accuracy loss. The extra copy raises weight memory by about 50%, but the overall memory impact is smaller (impact on overall memory usage is much smaller).
- **Loss scaling:** The loss is multiplied by a scale factor before backpropagation so that tiny gradients don't round to zero in FP16. The gradients are divided by the same factor before the weight update. Without loss scaling, these small but important gradient values would become zeros, leading to training divergence.
- **FP16 products accumulated in FP32:** Matrix-multiply products are accumulated in FP32 and then stored as FP16. The half-precision arithmetic accumulates into single-precision outputs, which are converted to half-precision before storing to memory.

The paper's experiments span image classification, object detection, speech, and language models. Reported results show FP32-level accuracy across these tasks, with loss scaling especially needed for some detection and recurrent models.


REMINDER: You MUST include the sources above in your response to the user using markdown hyperlinks.

**Publication date:** September 10, 2025 (by Horace He, with others at Thinking Machines)

1. **Is "concurrency + floating point" the main cause?** No. The post calls the hypothesis "not entirely wrong" but incomplete. It states that "concurrency (and atomic adds) end up being completely uninvolved in LLM inference nondeterminism." The post identifies the main cause as batch size varying with server load: "the load (and thus batch-size) nondeterministically varies!"

2. **Are typical forward-pass GPU matmul kernels run-to-run deterministic?** Yes, with a caveat. The post says "Thus, the forward pass in an LLM is in fact "run-to-run deterministic."" It also notes that matmul determinism is "not totally true," but "most common matmul implementations do have this property." Matmul kernels are still not batch-invariant.

3. **Where do atomic adds appear?** The post says "The only one commonly used in LLMs, however, is FlashAttention backward." The forward pass involves no atomic adds.

4. **Batch invariance and its cost:**
   - *Definition:* "the reduction order for each element must be fixed regardless of the batch-size of the kernel."
   - *Cost:* "Despite obtaining batch invariance, we only lose about 20% performance compared to cuBLAS." In the vLLM experiment, the deterministic setup was slower than the default (about 55 s vs. 26 s), and an improved attention kernel reduced this to about 42 s.

Oracle announced in September 2025 that GraalVM is leaving the Java release train. The Oracle post says GraalVM for JDK 24 was the final GraalVM release licensed and supported as part of Oracle Java SE Products. Oracle JDK 24 was the final release to include the experimental and optional Graal JIT. Oracle is also discontinuing GraalVM Early Adopter technology, including Native Image, for Java SE Product customers. Oracle recommends that Graal JIT users migrate to the Oracle JDK JIT. The reason given is that Oracle is shifting the GraalVM team's focus toward non-Java Graal languages such as GraalPy and GraalJS.

On Project Galahad, the results don't include an official status update after the September announcement. The most recent material is from the 2025 OpenJDK mailing list. In April 2025, one participant wrote that Project Galahad is in progress and they are working on the galahad branch. Another said they didn't know why they haven't done so yet, meaning Graal JIT hadn't been merged into mainline OpenJDK. Galahad's original goal was to focus on the continued development and integration of the Graal just-in-time (JIT) compiler as an alternative to the existing HotSpot JIT compiler. Based on these results, I can't confirm whether Galahad is still active or whether the Graal JIT has been upstreamed.

Links: [{"title":"LockSupport.parkNanos() Under the Hood and the Curious Case of Parking","url":"https://hazelcast.com/?p=4220"},{"title":"locksupportparknanos under the hood and the curiou 1","url":"https://dzone.com/articles/locksupportparknanos-under-the-hood-and-the-curiou-1"},{"title":"LockSupport.parkNanos() Under the Hood and the Curious Case of Parking","url":"https://hazelcast.com/blog/locksupport-parknanos-under-the-hood-and-the-curious-case-of-parking/"},{"title":"RFR: 8307483: New micros for j.u.c.LockSupport [v3]","url":"https://mail.openjdk.org/pipermail/core-libs-dev/2023-May/105871.html"},{"title":"Systems and methods for performing concurrency restriction and throttling over contended locks","url":"https://image-ppubs.uspto.gov/dirsearch-public/print/downloadPdf/11314562"},{"title":"Systems and methods for performing concurrency restriction and throttling over contended locks","url":"https://image-ppubs.uspto.gov/dirsearch-public/print/downloadPdf/12182636"},{"title":"JDK 8305670","url":"https://bugs.openjdk.org/browse/JDK-8305670"},{"title":"Systems and methods for performing concurrency restriction and throttling over contended locks","url":"https://image-ppubs.uspto.gov/dirsearch-public/print/downloadPdf/10417056"},{"title":"developers.google.com","url":"https://developers.google.com/j2objc/javadoc/jre/reference/java/util/concurrent/locks/LockSupport.html"},{"title":"Malthusian Locks","url":"https://arxiv.org/pdf/1511.06035"}]

The search didn't turn up a specific published JMH ping-pong figure for `unpark` wake-up latency in microseconds, but it did surface several relevant findings.

- **Timer slack sets a floor on timed parks.** Hazelcast found that calling `LockSupport.parkNanos(10000)` would not return after 10 microseconds, but roughly after 50 μs. The cause is the Linux timer slack, which defaults to 50 µs. Lowering it through `/proc` brought the observed latency down to about 5 µs in their test. This affects timed parks, not necessarily `unpark` wake-ups.
- **Many idle threads can slow `unpark`.** An OpenJDK bug report says the issue appeared in JDK 10 with the introduction of Thread-SMR. The cause was a linear search in `ThreadsList::includes`, which made `unpark` slower when there were many threads. The bug was fixed in JDK 17.0.9 and later.
- **OpenJDK added microbenchmarks for this.** The JDK-8307483 review adds JMH benchmarks for `LockSupport` that create idle "sleepers" either before or after the worker threads, because thread creation order mattered for that bug.
- **Wake-up cost comes from the OS and CPU.** A Malthusian Locks paper notes that exit latency significantly impacts unpark latency – the time between an unpark(T) operation and the time when T returns from park. It also says deeper sleep states, while useful for energy consumption and turbo mode, may also increase the time it takes to wake a thread.

For actual numbers on your machine, you'd need to run your own JMH ping-pong benchmark, pinning threads and controlling for timer slack and CPU idle states.

16:An incubator module is identified by the jdk.incubator. prefix in its module name, whether the module exports an incubating API or contains an incubating tool.
17:An incubating API is identified by the jdk.incubator. prefix in its exported package names. An incubating API is exported only by an incubator module.
18:An incubating tool may use the jdk.incubator prefix in the tool name invoked on the command line, but is not required to.
19:If an incubating API is standardized in the Java SE Platform, or otherwise promoted to some stable mode of existence in the JDK, then its packages will be renamed and then exported from a non-incubator module. Early adopters will at the very minimum need to change their import statements, and may need to refactor their uses if the API changes more substantially. Similarly, if an incubating tool is promoted to some stable mode of existence, then early adopters may need to change any invoking scripts in order to account for changes in the tool's functionality and command line interface.
40:Incubator modules must export incubating APIs only, i.e., packages in the jdk.incubator namespace. Consequently:
46:Incubator modules are part of the JDK run-time image produced by the standard JDK build. However, by default, incubator modules are not resolved for applications on the class path. Furthermore, by default, incubator modules do not participate in service binding for applications on the class path or the module path.
47:Applications on the class path must use the --add-modules command-line option to request that an incubator module be resolved. Applications developed as modules can specify requires or requires transitive dependences upon an incubator module directly. (Some incubator modules, such as those offering command-line tools, may forego exporting any packages, and instead provide service implementations so that tools can be accessed programatically. It is usually not recommended to require a module that exports no packages, but it is necessary in this case in order to resolve the incubator module, and have its service providers participate in service binding.)
48:During the JDK build, incubator modules must be packaged into jmod files with the --do-not-resolve-by-default option of the jmod tool, so that they are not in the default set of root modules for the unnamed module. This makes them, in effect, "opt-in". Also, the --warn-if-resolved=incubating option must be passed to the jmod tool, so that a warning is issued at compile time, link time, and run time if the incubator module is resolved. This warning can be suppressed at compile time, but not at other times.
52:Many new APIs wish to integrate with the java.* and javax.* APIs of the Java SE Platform, but during incubation, an API must reside jdk.incubator. namespace and so "stands apart" from the SE APIs. Links: [{"title":"VectorBox enabling","url":"https://mail.openjdk.org/pipermail/panama-dev/2017-November/000786.html"},{"title":"VectorBox enabling","url":"https://mail.openjdk.org/pipermail/panama-dev/2017-November/000787.html"},{"title":"Intrinsics For Vector API","url":"https://mail.openjdk.org/pipermail/panama-dev/2017-August/000659.html"},{"title":"VectorBox enabling","url":"https://mail.openjdk.org/pipermail/panama-dev/2017-November/000789.html"},{"title":"On vector box elimination","url":"https://mail.openjdk.org/pipermail/panama-dev/2017-December/000840.html"},{"title":"Intrinsics For Vector API","url":"https://mail.openjdk.org/pipermail/panama-dev/2017-August/000663.html"},{"title":"VectorBox enabling","url":"https://mail.openjdk.org/pipermail/panama-dev/2017-November/000785.html"},{"title":"UTF-8 Validation with the Vector API (Performance)","url":"https://mail.openjdk.org/pipermail/panama-dev/2021-March/012375.html"},{"title":"Vector Intrinsics & Boxing Problems?","url":"https://mail.openjdk.org/pipermail/panama-dev/2020-December/011651.html"},{"title":"[vector] RFR (L): Vector box elimination improvements","url":"https://mail.openjdk.org/pipermail/panama-dev/2018-February/001030.html"}]

The search turned up mailing-list threads from the Panama/Vector API project, mostly from 2017 to 2021. They describe the same family of problem, but they predate current JDK releases, so check them against modern C2 behavior.

- **VectorBox left in place:** A 2017 thread reports that with late inlining disabled, a debug flag printed a message saying a VectorBox was not eliminated due to its uses. The author found the box was removed when late inlining was on, and asked why the behavior differed. When late inlining is enabled, the VectorBox is eliminated as desired because no equivalent uncommon_trap is inserted.
- **Boxes forced to materialize:** The same thread lists remaining limits. If VectorBox is used by any non-intrinsified calls, stores to heap, or runtime calls via deopt, it will generate an object at the original call site.
- **Phi merges block elimination:** A December 2017 post on box elimination says escape analysis does not cover control flow. EA implementation in C2 doesn't cover control flow, so *both* o1 & o2 will be conservatively marked as non-scalarizable. The proposed workaround is reboxing through a fresh box, which the author says removes the original allocation once it has not leaked.
- **2018 improvements:** A February 2018 review of box-elimination changes lists merge-through-phi and reboxing transformations, plus rematerialization at safepoints, as the core of the optimization.
- **Constant vectors and phis:** A 2021 thread reports that a zero vector built from the species, instead of the idiomatic constant, caused about a 7x slowdown with many spills in the hot loop. Paul Sandoz noted Vectors held in final fields of LookupTables might not be treated as constant. A 2020 thread reports that a single branch in a loop sharply reduced throughput. Vladimir Ivanov offered an experimental patch on a branch for that case.

None of the results mention "loop phi species not constant" as a specific diagnostic message, so I couldn't confirm that exact wording. The results also don't show whether these issues are fixed in current JDKs. For that, check the current JDK's Vector API (jdk.incubator.vector) release notes and the panama-dev archive for recent posts.

Generating Fast Matrix Multiplication Kernels Using the Scalable Matrix Extension","url":"https://arxiv.org/pdf/2409.18779"},{"title":"github.com","url":"https://github.com/michel2323/libxsmm"}]

The SC16 paper is "LIBXSMM: Accelerating Small Matrix Multiplications by Runtime Code Generation," listed on the conference's session page. The authors are Alexander Heinecke, Greg Henry, Maxwell Hutchinson, and Hans Pabst, according to a University of Illinois course slide deck.

- **Problem and approach:** The paper argues that small matrix multiplications underpin many scalable simulation codes, and that math libraries or compilers are unlikely to deliver the best kernel performance for them. It presents a library with high-performance small matrix multiplications for x86 vector extensions up to Intel AVX-512, and uses just-in-time compilation to build only the kernel variant needed at runtime.
- **Caching:** The slides note that generated code is cached to amortize compilation cost. A separate CP2K paper reports that generated code is kept for the runtime of an application and is ready for call at a rate of 20M-40M dispatches per second.
- **Earlier precursor:** A 2015 SC poster by the same group describes a modular design that separates a frontend (routine selection) from a backend (specific xGEMM code generation).

I ran one search, so I did not verify the paper's own benchmark numbers or read the full PDF. The session page is the primary source for the title and abstract; the author list comes from the slides.

The paper is Kazushige Goto and Robert van de Geijn's "Anatomy of High-Performance Matrix Multiplication," published in ACM Trans. Math. Softw., 34 (3): 12:1--12:25 (May 2008). Its DOI is 10.1145/1356052.1356053.

The search results support these points about the paper:

- **Scope:** It explains the principles behind the matrix-matrix multiplication in the GotoBLAS library. Its main focus is the macro-level layering around a high-performance inner kernel, with the micro-level kernel design treated as secondary (implementing matrix multiplication so that near-optimal performance is attained requires a thorough understanding of how the operation must be layered at the macro level).
- **Packing and the inner kernel:** The analysis assumes the inner kernel works with a packed block Ã that resides in the L1 cache (It assumes that this inner-kernel computes with a matrix Ã that resides in the level-1 (L1) cache.). The paper also treats the cost of moving data between RAM, cache, and registers.
- **Micro-kernel:** Optimized GEMM micro-kernels are typically written in assembly rather than a high-level language, as cited in later work (optimized GEMM implementations typically do not express the microkernel in a high-level language; it is typically expressed directly in assembly language).
- **Register blocking:** The BLIS follow-up work describes the register block sizes as being chosen within the micro-kernel and fixed afterward, usually reflected in the degree of assembly-level loop unrolling (the developer also chooses a set of register block sizes, which subsequently do not change since their values are typically reflected in the degree of assembly-level loop unrolling within the micro-kernel implementation).

The search returned the paper's PDF, bibliographic records, and later papers that cite it, but not its full text on the register-blocking details. For those, the PDF at cs.utexas.edu/~flame/pubs/GotoTOMS_final.pdf is the primary source.

toolu_016kPLZa1U2ov3rMyQS1jNpm.prompt: Quote the error bounds for naive (recursive) summation, pairwise summation, and Kahan summation (worst-case and root-mean-square), and which libraries use pairwise summation (NumPy, Julia). Note the references cited (Higham 1993).

content.content:
**Error bounds** (ε = machine precision, n = number of terms)

| Method | Worst case | Root-mean-square (random errors) |
|---|---|---|
| Naive (sequential) | "roundoff errors that grow at worst as O(εn)" | "naive summation has a root mean square relative error that grows as O(εn)" |
| Pairwise | "Its worst-case roundoff errors grow asymptotically as at most O(ε log n)" | "pairwise summation has an error that grows as O(εlog n) on average" |
| Kahan | "has a worst-case error of roughly O(ε), independent of n" | Not stated in the article |

The article notes that Kahan's worst-case error is "independent of n" but "requires several times more arithmetic operations." It gives no RMS bound for Kahan summation.

**Libraries:** "Pairwise summation is the default summation algorithm in NumPy and the Julia technical-computing language." The article says it was found to have comparable speed to naive summation because of a large base case. It also lists the HPCsharp library for C# and the D standard library as other implementations.

**Reference:** The worst-case bounds come from Higham, Nicholas J. (1993), "The accuracy of floating point summation," *SIAM Journal on Scientific Computing*, 14(4): 783–799. The RMS/random-walk results are attributed to Manfred Tasche and Hansmartin Zeuner, *Handbook of Analytic-Computational Methods in Applied Mathematics* (CRC Press, 2000).

**Abstract claims:**
- **Range:** BF16 covers the same range as FP32, described as "the range of values it can represent is the same as that of IEEE 754 floating-point format (FP32)."
- **No hyperparameter tuning:** The authors contrast this with FP16, which they say needs tuning. They state that "no hyper-parameter tuning is required for convergence" for BF16.
- **Loss scaling:** The page does not mention loss scaling.
- **Results:** BF16 reportedly reaches state-of-the-art results "across domains as FP32 tensors" in the same number of iterations, with no hyperparameter changes. The domains are image classification, speech recognition, language modeling, generative networks, and industrial recommendation systems.
- **Implementation:** The authors emulated BF16 in TensorFlow, Caffe2, IntelCaffe, and Neon.
- **FP32 accumulation and master weights:** The page content does not address either topic.

**Publication date:** October 14, 2026.

38:In 2000, Samuel Larsen and Saman Amarasinghe presented Exploiting Superword Level Parallelism with Multimedia Instruction Sets. They auto-vectorize basic blocks, so that multiple scalar operations can be packed into a SIMD vector instruction. Their algorithm can thus be used on any program part that does not contain control flow (no branching / merging, no If, etc). The only requirement is that it has sufficient parallelism. For loops, this can often be achieved by loop unrolling. That way, one can fuse together multiple loop iterations into one basic block, and exploit the potential parallelism between different loop iterations.
39:The algorithm has been implemented in the HotSpot JVM. However, there are a few things that have been altered for the implementation. It only applies the algorithm to loop bodies, after a few iterations of loop unrolling.

92:Given: the DAG with ops of a basic block (loop body, no control flow).
95:independent: two ops are independent if there is no path from one to the other. We can only pack independent ops into a SIMD vector, since they are executed concurrently, so one cannot use the other’s output in any way.
100:Note: isomorphism and independence are necessary conditions for SLP vectorization. They are useful to make “local” decisions about individual nodes in their graph-neighbourhood. However, they are not sufficient to ensure that there are no cycles. We will discuss this in more details later.
111:Algorithm Step 0: Loop Unrolling
112:As already explained earlier, the algorithm works on basic blocks. This can be the body of a loop (without any control flow). But it can be any basic block, even outside of loops.
113:The implementation in the HotSpot JVM currently only applies the SuperWord algorithm for loops. Since it is a JIT (just in time) compiler, one has to focus the time spent on optimizations to the places where it is most promising. That is most often loops.
114:To ensure that the full size of the SIMD vectors can be filled, one needs to unroll loops with at least a multiple of vector_width / sizeof(type). In the JVM code, this is further refined for each type. One will have to unroll less for an 8-byte long, than for a 2-byte short. Unrolling less means the algorithm has to process fewer noodes, and process them faster.
115:Still: the SLP algorithm also allows hand-unrolled loops (see example below).
126:The dependency graph now only consists of such memory edges, and all data edges from the C2 graph (dependencies data -> data, data -> memop, memop -> data).

152:It is also supposed to weight the gains made by executing operations in parallel, versus the potential costs of packing/unpacking if the inputs/outputs are not vectorizable.
156:We should only extend to non-memory nodes. If we also extend to memory nodes, then we may re-introduce loads/stores that we rejected, for example because of mis-alignment.

215:Note: dataI1 == dataI2 and dataF1 == dataF2. I only had to use two references so that C2 does not know this, and does not optimize away load after store.
217:Conclusion: independence on the pack level is a necessary condition, but not sufficient. We must explicitly check that the pack-graph does not introduce any cycles, so that we can guarantee that the output DAG is indeed acyclic, with the same semantics (same effect/results).

17:To access SME operations, the CPU must be in the streaming SVE (SSVE) mode. This is controlled by `smstart`/`smstop` instructions. The streaming mode has its own implementation defined vector length `VL`. Furthermore, the implementation is free to choose how much of core SVE instructions are supported in the streaming mode. The reason behind this complexity is to permit SME to be implemented via a separate hardware unit (coprocessor). The capabilities of this unit can be different from that of the main CPU core. For example, the SME coprocessor can be optimized for working with large data, favouring compute throughput over latency (best for HPC problems). The main CPU core instead can be optimized for latency and smaller problems (best for general-purpose programming). To add to the confusion, while SME builds on SVE, an implementation is allowed to support SME/SSVE but not SVE. This is the case for Apple M4, which supports SME version 2 (and a subset of SVE) when in streaming mode, but does not support SVE otherwise.
23:- Switching into the streaming mode makes regular SVE SIMD inaccessible and via versa
24:- An implementation might support streaming mode SVE, but not regular (non-streaming mode) SVE
